articles.title: Nike’s Air Max 1000 are almost entirely 3D-printed
articles.summary: Nike’s new Air Max 1000 are the company’s first 3D-printed shoes made from a single lightweight flexible material.
articles.body: Nike’s new Air Max 1000 are the company’s first shoes manufactured almost entirely using 3D printing. Debuting at ComplexCon this past weekend in Las Vegas, Nike collaborated with Zellerfeld — a company that already has expertise in 3D printing shoes — to create the Air Max 1000, but they’re not currently available to the general public. The Air Max 1000’s design is an updated take on the Air Max 1, which debuted in 1987 as Nike’s first shoe with an air cushion in the heel that was visible through a window in the midsole. That feature is carried forward to the new Air Max 1000, and although the air cushion itself isn’t 3D-printed, the rest of the shoe uses a single flexible material. [Image: Everything except the Air Max 1000’s air cushion is 3D-printed. By mixing layers with varying densities and textures, the outsole on the bottom of the Air Max 1000 remains firm and supportive, while the upper parts of the shoe are more flexible and comfortable, allowing them to be slipped on and off without the need for laces. [Media: The use of 3D printing also allowed Nike to realize the Air Max 1000’s unique contoured design, which the company says would have been impossible using traditional shoe manufacturing techniques. “As an innovator, what’s most exciting to me about the Air Max 1000 are the new solutions we can achieve with next-level manufacturing,” says John Hoke, Nike’s Chief Innovation Officer. Nike originally announced the Air Max 1000 in a solid bright red colorway, but influencers at the event later revealed additional colors of the shoe, including orange, white, blue, and black with a green air cushion. And while Nike distributed a small number of pairs of the Air Max 1000 at the event, wider availability was limited to 1,000 pairs that attendees could win the chance to preorder, according to Elliot Page, who also shared a brief video review of the shoes. Nike hasn’t revealed plans for a wider general release of the Air Max 1000, nor has it revealed what the pricing might be. But the 3D-printed shoes now available on Zellerfeld’s website range in price from $159 for a sandal design to almost $400 for a high-top. The Air Max 1000 aren’t the first time Nike has used 3D printing to make shoes. In 2017, the company debuted its VaporFly Elite Flyprint with a lighter and more breathable fabric material it claimed was the “first 3D-printed textile upper in performance footwear.” Other companies, such as Adidas, already sell shoes with 3D-printed midsoles. But like Nike, Adidas is also experimenting with shoes made entirely from 3D-printed materials, including its new Climacool24 that debuted in October.

articles.title: Google is open-sourcing its 3D emoji
articles.summary: Google is making its Noto Emoji 3D set available to everyone and offers a bit of insight into the design process for World Emoji Day.
articles.body: Now, if you want to, you can use Google’s 3D emoji in your own creations. The company shared some details about how it went about designing the little pictograms and why, as part of World Emoji Day on Friday. Things you might not necessarily worry about in a 2D illustration suddenly become very important when you’re talking about a 3D model. Is a smiley face a sphere? A mask? A flat disc? In addition to offering a behind-the-scenes look at Google’s design process, it also announced that it would be completely open-sourcing the emoji set: > We’re handing over raw .OBJ files to the community so they can use them to build immersive VR worlds, indie apps or weird memes. Exactly what kind of “immersive VR worlds” someone might want to build with a bunch of emojis is a bit of a mystery to me. But if the Emoji Movie is any indication, it won’t be good. Google’s Noto Emoji 3D made their debut in May and were met with 😬 reactions.

articles.title: I let Apple’s always-listening AI summarize my life for two weeks
articles.summary: Siri Recap is in beta, but after roughly two weeks of testing, it’s clear that prioritizing privacy has some pros and cons.
articles.body: Was it worth it? I’ve been asking myself this quite a bit over the last month or so while testing both the Amazon Bee Frontier and Siri Recap on the Apple Watch Ultra 4. Both enable a wearable to ambiently listen to your conversations and, using AI, summarize them for you. Why? So you can remember better and, hopefully, stay more present. The main difference is that Amazon’s Bee takes a maximalist (and frankly reality-bending) approach, whereas Apple is going for a more minimalist, privacy-first take. Both, however, require explicit disclosures to the people around you about recording what they say, and potentially follow-up explanations about how exactly this all works. This past week, I’ve been testing the Siri Recap beta to see if Apple’s is a less dystopian experience. Apple presents Siri Recap as a sort of backup notetaker. As a college student, perhaps you’re less concerned about writing down what a professor says and can just take in the lecture. Say you attend a parent-teacher conference solo. You can focus on the discussion and then whip out your phone later to reference what was said when explaining it to your spouse. These are fairly innocuous scenarios. But given the discourse around privacy and surveillance gadgets this year, it’s easy to imagine how always-listening devices could be misused. Apple has taken great care to create a version of this that at least considers that bystanders may feel uncomfortable knowing someone else’s Apple Watch may be taking notes on what they say. [Image: There are several customization options for when Siri Recap is turned on or off. The feature isn’t turned on by default — you have to opt in. Users can then program when the feature turns on. For example, only at the office between the hours of 1 to 2PM on weekdays. Unless saved, all recaps are also set to self-destruct after your choice of one, three, or seven days. Within the summaries, there’s no viewable transcript detailing who said what and when. That makes these recaps more difficult to use as “receipts” for arguments, court cases, or blackmail. There’s also no raw audio file that’s ever saved. Not to get too into the weeds, but the audio gets processed and then immediately deleted through a secure exclave within the 2026 Apple Watch’s S11 chip that’s inaccessible to Apple and other third parties. The vast majority of the processing is also done locally. Whatever does get sent to the cloud is done through Apple’s Private Cloud Compute. Because the feature requires this hardware, it’s impossible to use on older Apple Watches. It’s not perfect. Unlike Live Rewind, another audio intelligence feature, there’s no outward indicator or audio chime to signal recording intent. So, if you do decide to ethically disclose your usage, you have to be prepared to explain everything I just described if someone asks questions. Maybe that’s worth it — if Siri can be trusted to be truly helpful. [Image: This was a TikTok. My spouse would NEVER. The reality is that better privacy often means a less useful AI product. The more AI knows about you, the better the summaries from these devices tend to be. To preserve privacy, Apple prevents Siri from learning everything about you and the people in your life. For example, Siri Recap doesn’t train on your voice. Excellent for privacy! But that also means Siri has a much harder time discerning when you’re actually having a conversation. That leads to some funny but ultimately unhelpful recaps. For instance, I was watching a TikTok in which a chronically ill creator was updating their followers about being sent to the emergency room because of sepsis. Siri recapped that video as if I, or potentially someone I knew, had been sent to the ER. Another TikTok weighing in on an AITA Reddit thread got summarized as if I had discussed a shady homewrecker named Dana trying to seduce her bestie’s husband by wearing a glittery blue bikini top at a concert. Because attribution was stripped, the summary could read as if I were the guilty spouse returning between 2 and 3AM, covered in Dana’s glitter. In both instances, the lack of attribution also made the resulting summaries hilarious and confusing. Also, neither video was something I wanted or needed to remember. I suspect Siri summarized them because I was playing the audio out loud on my phone, which sits pretty close to my Apple Watch. There’s an easy workaround here. Siri Recap automatically turns off if you use headphones, meaning I could just eliminate recaps from podcasts, audiobooks, TV shows, etc., by always wearing my AirPods. But that’s me adjusting my behavior to accommodate Siri’s inability to discern when I’m talking. Another quirk: Siri doesn’t know what I want to remember or find memorable from a given conversation. I turned on Siri Recap during my briefing and demos for the new smart glasses from Google, Samsung, Gentle Monster, and Warby Parker. When I sat down to write, the resulting recap helped me remember the main topics discussed. I also found it useful that a handful of interview recaps were linked to a corresponding Voice Memos file. The thing is, Siri Recap heavily prioritizes restating the facts. That means bullet points tend to emphasize statistics, factoids, and dates. That’s useful in straightforward planning meetings, but less useful for what you might personally find to be a salient takeaway. For example, in an interview with a source, what I found most interesting was a personal anecdote and some strong opinions about RFK Jr. My Siri Recap from that interview omitted it in favor of more concrete details. [Image: I am not having ethical dilemmas over funding my independent documentary about a wealthy former athlete. This is the plot of an episode of The Rise and Fall of Reggie Dinkins. Meanwhile, personal conversations are rarely as straightforward. Work meetings often have agendas. Chats with friends and family can jump across a zillion topics in the span of 10 minutes. Plus, most of my conversations should be deleted from my brain to make room for the really important things. I didn’t need to see a detailed summary of what my spouse and I thought of the last episode of Nathan Fielder’s The Curse. (It was bonkers.) I’d love to never revisit a 20-minute argument with my cousin over hardwired versus battery-powered smoke detectors. (Too bad, the recap outlined the main points.) A recap of my spouse and me debating movie recommendations might be a useful recap, but it just says “seeking less anxiety-inducing media” and “refusing to ever watch Star Wars.” My recaps were also a lesson in why conversational context matters. Sometimes, Siri correctly assumes that gossip is irrelevant to the broader conversation at hand and omits it entirely. Other times, its blunt, matter-of-fact recaps of jokes or my friends venting read like an unhinged Regina George from Mean Girls building an AI-generated Burn Book. That inconsistency is why relying on AI to make judgment calls on your behalf feels unsettling. I keep getting stuck on what problem these features are meant to solve. Tech companies usually say ambient listening is meant to help jog our memories or to help us stay more present. Which brings me back to my initial question: Was it worth it? Did Apple’s efforts to protect privacy prove we can have our AI note-taking cake and eat it too? Outside a few work-related scenarios, I haven’t found Siri Recaps to be useful. Even writing this, I spent a lot of time scrolling to find a small handful of examples that I would want to discuss. On the plus side, I’m not terribly worried about people snooping through my recaps. Of the more than 50 recaps generated, I’m confident 90 percent would be gibberish for anyone but me. Conversely, I found more of what Amazon’s Bee generated to be “useful.” But after seeing Bee’s raw transcripts and summaries of every spoken moment in my life, I believe we’re not meant to live that way. I’ve since nuked all my Bee data. [Image: This is a mix of a Last Week Tonight episode and a conversation between my spouse and I. But even if I prefer Apple’s approach for privacy reasons, my gut says this tech isn’t the answer for jogging memories or staying present. Whenever I’ve forgotten things, the negative consequences have rarely — if ever — led to irrevocably changing my life for the worse. Usually, it’s a bitter lesson that’s forced me to grow and adapt. And anytime I’m not present in the moment, it’s usually because I’m on my phone. Ambient listening wearables can be helpful when used in low-stakes, straightforward situations where everyone consents. But for me, it’s often in little ways that have many less-invasive alternatives. I mean having to explain to the less tech-savvy people in my life that my Apple Watch now has this feature that recaps our conversations. Having to watch how their faces mull it over. Having to muster the will to answer their questions about how Apple handles privacy with this feature versus other devices I’ve tested. Having to smile when my spouse jokes about censoring their humor because of my job. Having to write in my work Slack that when my coworkers see me in the office, I am testing AI devices that may be recording any conversation, and that I am happy to turn them off if it makes them uncomfortable. Having to weigh whether I have enough bandwidth or time before every conversation with strangers to be thoughtful and ethical. Right now, there are no established cultural norms telling me how to easily pay this cost. All I know is that if I turn the feature off, I don’t have to think about it at all.

articles.title: Nimble enters the item-tracking market with eco-friendly luggage tags and keychains | TechCrunch
articles.summary: As Google takes on Apple in the item-tracking market, Nimble is hoping its trackable wallets, keychains, luggage tags, and passport covers stand out.
articles.body:
As Google steps up its competition with Apple in the item-tracking market, smaller brands are also looking to carve out a piece of the category. The latest entrant is Nimble , the sustainable accessories brand best known for its charging products.

Founded in 2018 by former Mophie executives, the California-based company announced Thursday that it’s expanding into the category with “Trace,” a seven-product collection of item trackers designed to blend tracking technology into everyday accessories.

Nimble’s new collection arrives as competition in the Bluetooth tracking market continues to heat up. Apple’s AirTag helped popularize the category, while Google recently introduced its first-party tracker, the $29 Pixel Tag, powered by its Find Hub network. Meanwhile, established third-party players, such as Chipolo and Pebblebee , continue to expand their lineups.

Nimble is taking a slightly different approach. Rather than introducing another stand-alone tracker to attach to a set of keys or slip into a bag, the company has integrated tracking technology directly into practical accessories, including wallets, keychains, luggage tags, and passport covers.

The lineup includes seven products, ranging from the $14.95 Trace Tag, which features a replaceable coin-cell battery, to the $49.95 Trace Folio, a passport cover with built-in rechargeable tracking. Other options include the Trace Keyfob ($19.95), Trace Slim Wallet Card ($29.95), Trace Keychain ($29.95), Trace Luggage Tag ($39.95), and Trace Wallet ($39.95).

The entire collection is compatible with both Apple’s Find My and Google’s Find Hub networks.

Ross Howe, co-founder and CEO of Nimble, told us that the company’s approach is designed to differentiate its products from traditional trackers.

“Most locators are built as utility gadgets, not as things you want to own. Few were asking why the locator couldn’t just be the nice object itself. So, for example, we made a wallet findable instead of making a tracker that fits a wallet. We also thought more options should be rechargeable.”

The Trace Luggage Tag and Trace Folio are arguably the most interesting products in the collection. Dedicated luggage tags and passport covers with built-in tracking remain relatively uncommon, giving Nimble an opportunity to stand out in a market. There are only a few alternatives, including Spotminder’s $59 passport cover with Apple Find My support, which is $10 more than Nimble’s option. Knog Scout offers a luggage tag, although I find its design a little too bulky.

Rechargeability is another appealing aspect of Nimble’s new collection. Several models support USB-C or wireless charging, offering an alternative to the disposable batteries found in many traditional trackers. Howe says battery life lasts for “months,” with the Trace Keyfob, for example, rated for approximately six months on a charge.

Sustainability is another major part of Nimble’s pitch. Staying true to its roots, the company has incorporated eco-friendly materials throughout the collection, including recycled plastics and plant-based, vegan aloe leather. The products have also undergone third-party testing for chemicals of concern.

“We’ve spent the last two years going through the chemistry of our products line by line to remove or limit as many harmful ingredients as possible. Trace is the first collection designed specifically to meet these higher standards. We’re not 100% yet, but the independent labs checking our work will help us get there,” Howe said.

The collection is available now through its website and Amazon. All seven products come in five color options: Black, Stone, Tangerine, Plum, and Teal.

articles.title: The Analogue 3D can now update itself over Wi-Fi
articles.summary: The latest firmware for the Analogue 3D activates the console’s dormant Wi-Fi hardware so it can automatically download and install future updates itself.
articles.body: Analogue has long been good at expanding the features and functionality of its consoles through regular firmware updates, but installing those updates has always required moving files around with a memory card. That’s no longer the case with the Analogue 3D, the company’s modernized version of the Nintendo 64. Although the console has had Wi-Fi hardware since day one, it’s only now been finally activated through the last update you’ll need to install with a memory card. Analogue on Wednesday released the version 1.6.0 firmware for the Analogue 3D, adding support for 2.4GHz, 5GHz, mixed, and hidden Wi-Fi networks. Once the update is installed, the Wi-Fi setup process will begin automatically when the console is booted, but there’s now an added Wi-Fi section in the Analogue 3D’s settings menu for updating passwords and other details later. The console’s new Wi-Fi capabilities add a couple of useful features at launch. In the future, the Analogue 3D will be able to download and install firmware updates so it automatically keeps itself up to date. The new wireless capabilities enable automatic date and time settings based on your time zone, too, and in the privacy section of the console’s settings menu, you’ll now find an option for sharing “anonymous usage and analytics data” with Analogue to help further improve its hardware.

articles.title: Apple Photos AI watermark can tag your real pictures
articles.summary: Apple Photos now embeds an invisible SynthID watermark in images edited with Apple Intelligence tools like Clean Up, Extend and Reframe in iOS 27.2.
articles.body: You take a great family photo, but there's one problem. Someone you don't know walked into the background. So you open Apple Photos, use Clean Up to remove the person and save your picture. Problem solved, right? Well, there's something new happening behind the scenes. With iOS 27.2, Apple Photos can now add an invisible AI watermark to pictures you edit using certain Apple Intelligence tools. You won't see it on your screen. And if you share the photo, the person receiving it probably won't notice anything different either. But the watermark could still be there. Apple introduced the feature in its Oct. 26 update. It uses Google's SynthID technology to identify images created or modified with artificial intelligence. Even a photo you took yourself can receive this hidden marker after certain AI edits. So how does it work, and what does it mean for the photos you share? Missed CyberGuy LIVE? Watch the replay and discover 5 ways to travel smarter and save money. Our free CyberGuy LIVE class, 5 Ways to Travel Smarter and Save Money, has ended, but you can still watch the full replay. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five practical ways to protect your phone and personal information, avoid common travel scams, find better deals, save money on bookings and use technology to make your travels easier and less stressful. No technical experience is needed. Watch the free replay + downloadable checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com. STOP LOSING PHOTO QUALITY WHEN YOU SHARE PICTURES Why Apple Photos is adding invisible AI watermarks AI photo editing has come a long way. What once required complicated software can now take a few taps on your phone. That's convenient when you want to improve a picture. However, it also makes it harder to tell what's real. Someone can remove an important detail from a photo without leaving an obvious trace. AI can even generate parts of a scene that the camera never captured. Apple's new watermarking feature gives people a way to tell when AI has been used to create or change an image. According to Apple's official support documentation, certain Apple Intelligence tools now add a hidden SynthID watermark when you create or edit images. SynthID is technology developed by Google. It embeds a digital signal into an image that compatible detection tools can recognize. The watermark doesn't visibly change your photo. There's no stamp across the bottom or warning in the corner. Instead, the marker remains hidden unless someone checks the image with a SynthID detector. Which Apple Photos tools add an AI watermark? Apple says the feature applies to certain Apple Intelligence tools starting with iOS 27.2. Here's where you might encounter it. 1. Clean Up removes unwanted people or objects Clean Up lets you erase distractions from your pictures. Maybe someone wandered into your vacation photo. Or perhaps there's an object in the background you wish you could remove. You can use Clean Up to erase that distraction while AI fills in the missing area. With iOS 27.2, some photos edited this way can receive a SynthID watermark. However, Apple doesn't say that every small edit will trigger one. The watermark can depend on the changes made to the image. 2. Extend creates new background beyond your photo Have you ever taken a picture and realized you were standing too close? Apple's Extend tool can help by generating additional scenery beyond the original edges of your photo. For example, you might have cropped out part of a building. Extend can generate additional background to make the composition look better. The result may look like you captured a wider shot in the first place. However, because AI creates part of the finished image, the photo can receive a hidden SynthID watermark. We've previously explained how Extend works in our article on fixing badly framed photos after you take them. 3. Reframe changes the perspective of a picture Apple also includes Spatial Reframing, called Reframe in Photos, among the tools covered by SynthID. Reframe lets you change the apparent perspective of a picture after you've taken it. You can adjust the angle or shift the composition while Apple Intelligence generates the necessary visual information. That can make a photo look quite different from what your camera originally captured. And because AI helps create that result, the edited image may carry a watermark. 4. Image Playground and Image Wand create AI images Apple's watermarking feature also covers images generated using Image Playground and Image Wand. Image Playground lets you create images with AI using descriptions or other visual inputs. Image Wand can turn a rough sketch into a more developed image. Since these tools generate visual content, their inclusion makes sense. But Apple's decision to mark certain edits to genuine photos raises a more interesting question. Should a real photo receive an AI marker because you removed one distracting object? NEW YORK MAKES HISTORY WITH FIRST-OF-ITS-KIND LAW REGULATING AI-POWERED COMMERCIALS How to check whether a photo has Apple's AI watermark You might be wondering whether there's an easy way to see if a photo contains one of these hidden markers. There is, although you'll need to use an online detector. Apple recommends Google's SynthID Detector, which can analyze an uploaded image for the watermark. Check a photo for a SynthID watermark One thing to understand: finding a watermark doesn't automatically mean a photo is fake. It simply indicates that AI was involved in creating or modifying the image. And the reverse is also true. If no watermark appears, that doesn't prove the picture is genuine. Other AI image generators may not use SynthID. Detection can also have limitations. I would also be careful about uploading private family pictures or sensitive images to any online service. Review how the service handles uploaded files before submitting them. Will Apple add watermarks to your older photos? Apple says photos created or edited before the 27.2 update won't automatically receive a new SynthID watermark from Apple. So you don't have to worry about the update going through your entire photo library and adding markers to everything. However, that changes if you open an older picture and edit it using one of the supported AI tools. For example, you could take a photo from five years ago and use Extend to improve the framing today. The newly edited version may then receive the invisible watermark. Apple has also expanded this feature beyond iPhones. According to the company, SynthID support begins with these software versions: iOS 27.2, iPadOS 27.2, macOS 27.2 and visionOS 27.2. Keep in mind that the software update and Apple Intelligence have different device requirements. OPENAI CHILD SAFETY TOOLS TARGET AI-GENERATED ABUSE Which iPhones support Apple's AI photo tools? You'll need an Apple Intelligence-compatible iPhone to use the editing features that trigger these watermarks. Apple Intelligence works on the iPhone 15 Pro and iPhone 15 Pro Max, along with iPhone 16 models and newer compatible iPhones. The standard iPhone 15 can install iOS 27.2, but it doesn't support these Apple Intelligence editing features. Availability may also depend on your region and language. To check for the latest software update: Can invisible watermarks help you spot fake photos? I like the idea of giving people another way to question what they're seeing online. But there's an important limitation. Let's say you use Clean Up to remove someone standing behind your family in a vacation photo. Now compare that with an AI-generated picture showing an event that never happened. Both images could carry SynthID watermarks, even though the circumstances are very different. The detector may identify AI involvement. However, it won't necessarily explain what was changed or how significant those changes were. That's a pretty big limitation when you're trying to decide whether to trust an image. There's also the issue of AI-generated pictures that have no detectable watermark. So, while SynthID can provide a useful clue, it shouldn't be your only way of evaluating a suspicious photo. If a picture online seems questionable, look for the original source. You can also use a reverse image search to see where a photo originally appeared and whether earlier versions exist. Kurt's key takeaways I can see why Apple is doing this. AI has gotten so good at changing photos that it's becoming harder to know what you're actually looking at. And I think that's a real concern. At the same time, I like having tools that can fix a great picture when someone walks into the background. Why should that photo get the same kind of watermark as a picture created entirely by AI? That's where I think Apple could do better. I'd love to see a way to check a photo and find out exactly what AI changed. Was it something minor, or did someone completely alter what happened? That's what I'd want to know before deciding whether to trust what I'm seeing. Should Apple put a hidden AI watermark on your personal photos simply because you removed something from the background? Or should these markers be reserved for images that AI creates entirely? Let us know by writing to us at CyberGuy.com. articles.title: The Verge’s 2026 fitness and wellness gift guide
articles.summary: Looking for a gift that encourages healthier habits? We’ve rounded up our favorite fitness gadgets and wellness gear, from open-ear headphones to massage guns.
articles.body: We could all use a hand when it comes to being more mindful about our health and fitness. articles.summary: Apple’s vice president of camera software engineering Jon McCormack reportedly left the company in October, according to Bloomberg.
articles.body: Jon McCormack, Apple’s vice president of camera software engineering, left the company last month, Bloomberg reports. Its sources say McCormack retired “at the end of October after more than eight years at the company.” Apple reportedly has not yet named a new VP to step in for McCormack, who oversaw its Camera and Photos apps, and the tech that defined generations of photos and the photography and editing experience on Apple’s devices. McCormack played a major role in defining how iPhone photos look, and he was always ready to get into the weeds with reporters after iPhone events. In 2024, he told The Verge that Apple sees a photo as “a personal celebration of something that really, actually happened.” The departure follows John Ternus taking over for Tim Cook as Apple’s CEO in September. Apple has had other major leadership changes recently, including Phil Schiller stepping down as head of the App Store and Apple events and Steve Smith stepping in as the company’s new M&A and corporate development boss.

articles.title: Avião declara emergência no Paraná após fumaça em bateria de lítio | G1
articles.standfirst: O avião saiu de Pato Branco, no Sudoeste do Paraná, com destino a Curitiba. Aeronave retornou ao aeroporto e Corpo de Bombeiros verificou que fumaça saia de bateria de lítio de cadeira de rodas. Ninguém se feriu.
articles.summary: Voo de Pato Branco para Curitiba declarou emergência após fumaça de uma bateria de lítio de cadeira de rodas ser detectada no porão; os 60 passageiros passam bem.
articles.body:
Um avião comercial que saiu do Aeroporto Regional de Pato Branco Professor Juvenal Loureiro Cardoso, no Sudoeste do Paraná, com destino a Curitiba, capital do estado, declarou emergência e precisou retornar logo após a decolagem por suspeita de fumaça no porão da aeronave. A situação foi registrada na tarde desta sexta-feira (20).

O voo era realizado pela Azul Linhas Aéreas, segundo informações da administração do aeroporto. Apesar do susto, ninguém ficou ferido. Os 60 passageiros que estavam no avião desembarcaram para que a situação fosse averiguada e, depois, o voo seguiu viagem para Curitiba.

Corpo de Bombeiros foi acionado para atender fumaça em avião — Foto: Foto: Antonio Neves/neves_spotters

Os dados da sala rádio do Aeroporto de Pato Branco registraram que a decolagem foi registrada às 15h34. Às 15h42, oito minutos depois, o comandante sentiu um forte cheiro de fumaça e declarou emergência. O pouso aconteceu apenas sete minutos depois da declaração de emergência, às 15h49.

Bateria de cadeira de rodas estava conectada e aqueceu

De acordo com Elenice Catafesta, diretora do Departamento de Transporte Aéreo da Prefeitura de Pato Branco, a tripulação identificou que a fumaça vinha da bateria de lítio de uma cadeira de rodas robótica.

Segundo o Corpo de Bombeiros, que foi acionado para atender a situação, o equipamento aqueceu, o que gerou a fumaça, mas não chegou a pegar fogo.

Bateria de lítio de cadeira de rodas aqueceu e causou fumaça — Foto: Foto: Aeroporto de Pato Branco

A diretora Catafesta contou que a cadeira era de um passageiro e estava no porão dianteiro da aeronave, e destacou ainda que a companhia aérea deu o aval para que o equipamento fosse transportado.

"Só que a bateria dela [da cadeira de rodas] estava conectada, o que, segundo os bombeiros, pode ter ocasionado o princípio de fumaça. A decisão do comandante foi de retornar, obviamente, para manter a segurança daquele voo. E aí retornando foi retirada a cadeira do porão, ela não seguiu viagem com a aeronave. Os passageiros desembarcaram, como protocolo de segurança, e depois foi feito o embarque novamente", explicou Catafesta.

O g1 tenta contato com a Azul Linhas Aéreas, mas não obteve retorno até a última atualização desta reportagem.

"O Aeroporto de Pato Branco afirma que adota os procedimentos necessários para garantir a segurança das operações", informou a instituição em nota.

Israel e Rodolffo desistem de decolar do aeroporto de Pato Branco devido a temporal

A dupla sertaneja Israel e Rodolffo também estava no aeroporto de Pato Branco nesta sexta-feira (20) e desistiu de embarcar por conta de uma tempestade que atingiu a cidade.

Em vídeo postado nas redes sociais, Rodolffo afirmou que a dupla chegou a entrar no avião, mas optaram por não seguir viagem após receberem informações de que as condições climáticas não estavam favoráveis.

"Tem que respeitar o clima, tem que respeitar o tempo. Não iremos mais hoje. Mas, graças a Deus, está tudo certo. Nós não temos compromisso hoje", afirmou.

articles.body: Samsung Electronics has promoted Hwang Sang-joon to president and head of its memory chip business as part of a management reshuffle, as the South Korean technology giant looks to strengthen its position in the fast-growing artificial intelligence semiconductor market. According to a report by Reuters, the company said that Hwang, who earlier headed the memory development, will now lead the oversee memory division. Samsung also added that the company expects Hwang to "help strengthen the competitiveness of memory products in the AI era." This appointment at Samsung comes at a time when the demand for AI infrastructure and data centres is increasing continuously and the sales of advanced memory chips is expected to witness a boost, which will help Samsung to deliver record earnings from its semiconductor operations.AI chip demand fuels record profitsThe Reuters report further revealed that the changes at the Samsung management came after a strong quarter. The South Korean electronics giant recently reported a 15-fold jump in quarterly semiconductor profit, driven by robust demand for AI-related chips and a supply crunch that pushed up prices across the sector. The company said that it promoted executives who played an important role in achieving the record semiconductor results and also helped in strengthening technological competitiveness.Despite the leadership shake-up, Vice Chairman and Co-CEO Jun Young-hyun will continue to lead Samsung's broader Device Solutions division, which includes memory, logic and foundry businesses. Samsung said Jun will focus on strengthening future growth areas, including its contract chip manufacturing operations.More leadership changes in chip divisionSamsung also promoted Cho Sang-yeun, who previously headed its US chip operations, to lead the System LSI Business, which designs logic semiconductors for technology companies. The company said Cho's global customer relationships would help expand the customer base for the System LSI division.Meanwhile, Lee Jong-myeong, who previously oversaw chip process development for memory and foundry operations, was named chief technology officer of the Device Solutions division. Industry observers said the latest appointments could help Samsung expand its foundry business and attract a broader range of customers in the AI market.New mobile business chief appointedAlongside changes in its semiconductor business, Samsung named President Choi Won-joon as the new head of its mobile devices division. articles.summary: Waymo and Serve Robotics are ending their exclusive deals with Uber, threatening the ridehail giant’s ambition to become the default app for autonomous vehicles and robot delivery.
articles.body: In a late August earnings call, Uber CEO Dara Khosrowshahi sounded optimistic about his company’s “very strong” partnership with Waymo, the global leader in autonomous robotaxis. The two companies had been working together for years in several cities — including exclusively in Austin and Atlanta — and things were going swimmingly, according to Khosrowshahi. “We believe we’ll continue to operate next year in those marketplaces,” he gushed. “It’s a terrific product, and the on-the-ground partnership continues to be very strong.” The partnership would turn out to be more brittle than Khosrowshahi let on. Several weeks later, Waymo co-CEO Tekedra Mawakana revealed in an interview that her company planned to end its exclusive robotaxi partnership with Uber, calling the mixed-fleet experience a “crapshoot” for its own customers. Starting in January 2028, riders in Austin and Atlanta will be able to use the Waymo app to hail driverless rides directly. The unlikely partnership, it would seem, was coming to an end. Waymo isn’t alone in souring on its experience in the Uber ecosystem. Serve Robotics, which operates thousands of sidewalk delivery robots in dozens of US cities, recently announced it would not renew its partnership with Uber Eats when it expires in 2027. AI chatbots may be getting all the attention these days, but robotaxis and sidewalk bots are the ones putting in the physical work. Autonomy is now a true commercial business — albeit an unprofitable one — and the companies building the robots no longer want an intermediary standing between them and their customers. That’s bad news for Uber, which aspires to be the premier robot-powered ridehail and delivery app on the planet. After Waymo and Serve realized their respective visions for how to operate and bring autonomy to the world differed from Uber’s, the mega platform’s quest looked to be in doubt. “This thing is real. It used to be a dream,” Serve Robotics CEO Ali Kashani told me recently. “And now you see Waymos everywhere, you see Serve robots everywhere. So some of the tensions about how that future is going to shake out [are] now actually coming to light.” [Image: Waymo won’t be exclusive to Uber in Austin, Texas, and Atlanta after January 2028. At first, Uber’s pitch to robotaxi and sidewalk robot operators was simple: Let us help you get off the ground by connecting your vehicles to our massive customer base and encouraging a skeptical public to give them a try. Initially, it seemed like a pretty good deal. If you’re a cash-strapped autonomous vehicle startup, why not piggyback on Uber’s platform, where hundreds of millions of people summon cars or order something delivered every day? “I call this the Trojan horse,” said Harry Campbell, who writes about the autonomous vehicle industry in his newsletter, The Driverless Digest. “[Uber] introduces the Waymo product to a bunch of actual regular users and riders of Uber who would have never considered AVs.” It wasn’t just Waymo and Serve that saw the benefit — more than 30 companies around the world have deals with Uber to feature their autonomous vehicles on its app. Amazon’s Zoox just launched with Uber in Las Vegas. China’s WeRide has vehicles operating on the Uber app in Abu Dhabi, Dubai, Riyadh, and Madrid. Avride, the tech startup that spun out of Russia’s Yandex, has both autonomous vehicles and sidewalk robots active on Uber and Uber Eats in Dallas. This is all part of Uber’s big play to become the default robotaxi and robot delivery app in the world, Khosrowshahi said on that August earnings call. Not just one or two companies — dozens. By 2028, Uber says it expects to have “tens of thousands” of unsupervised AVs, across more than 50 cities. And citing a recent analysis by Jeffries, Uber notes that in cities where robotaxis have been operating for a while (like San Francisco, Phoenix, and Los Angeles), the company’s business is actually growing faster — and capturing a bigger slice of the ride-hailing market — than in the rest of the country. "“[Uber] introduces the Waymo product to a bunch of actual regular users and riders of Uber who would have never considered AVs.”" - Harry Campbell “We want to make sure that we’re not dependent on one partner,” Khosrowshahi said in August. “We’re absolutely seeing a plethora of newer players in the AV ecosystem, just like you see in the foundation model space.” The only problem with that strategy is that partners eventually get antsy and want to split off on their own, Campbell said. “Waymo, I think, kind of held the cards and tried this experiment with Uber,” he said. “And within about six to 12 months, I think they knew it wasn’t working that well.” One of Waymo’s biggest problems was consistency. Uber’s theory was that customers could hail a ride and get paired with either a robotaxi or a human driver, whichever was closer. But as Waymo discovered, many riders preferred to know exactly what they were getting. “Early in adoption, predictability matters because many consumers are still forming their first impressions of autonomous vehicles,” TC Eley, an assistant professor of management information systems at the Villanova School of Business, told me in an email. “If riders specifically choose a robotaxi but receive a human driver, they lose an opportunity to learn about the technology on their own terms.” The flip side can also be true. “If [riders] do not want to ride in a robotaxi but are given one, this first impression may lead to the customer having a negative experience and not wanting to ride in an AV in the future,” Eley added. Uber has since pushed back on the idea that it wasn’t willing to adapt to Waymo’s needs. According to Bloomberg, the ridehail company pitched the idea of a dedicated robotaxi button in its app for Austin and Atlanta — but Waymo declined the offer. (A Waymo spokesperson didn’t reply to a request for comment.) Serve, which operates more than 2,000 sidewalk robots as the second-largest autonomous fleet in the US behind Waymo, illustrates a similar dynamic. Rather than renew its partnership with Uber Eats, the company launched a direct developer API allowing any small business to build its own robot delivery service using Serve’s fleet. The decision, according to Kashani, was largely economic. Delivery apps like DoorDash and Uber Eats take a massive 15 percent to 30 percent cut on every order, largely because paying human couriers is expensive. By letting businesses connect directly to its fleet through software, Serve wants to let local shops — like bakeries, florists, and pharmacies — add robot delivery straight to their own websites and checkout registers without paying steep middleman fees. “At least in our case, there was a different vision for how we wanted to operate and kind of bring this to the world versus how Uber wanted to,” Kashani said. “They’re doing what’s right for their business, and we’re going to do what’s right for ours.” In a statement, Uber spokesperson Noah Edwardsen said the fault lies with Serve, not Uber. “We believe autonomy will be a key part of the future of both delivery and mobility, and we continue to scale with many partners around the world,” Edwardsen said. “Beginning in early 2026, we repeatedly raised concerns to Serve about operational performance and reliability, and unfortunately performance did not improve to the level we required.” [Image: Uber once aspired to build its own self-driving cars — an effort that ended in tragedy. It wasn’t long ago that Waymo and Uber were locked in a bitter standoff over the future of autonomous vehicles. In 2017, the Alphabet-owned company sued Uber over allegations of trade secret theft and patent infringement. The case went to trial a year later but ended abruptly when the two sides reached a surprise settlement after just a week of testimony. Uber later admitted that it misappropriated some of Waymo’s tech and agreed to license it for future use. Anthony Levandowski, a former Google engineer, was sentenced to 18 months in prison for stealing Waymo’s trade secrets. (He was later pardoned by President Donald Trump.) Infamously, Uber once aspired to develop its own fleet of robotaxis with the intention of eventually replacing its human drivers, but the program was effectively dismantled after a woman was struck and killed by one of the company’s test vehicles in March 2018. Uber’s exit gave Waymo an opening. The company launched its own ridehail app, Waymo One, in late 2018, aiming to own the entire stack: building the tech, acquiring the customers, and controlling the rider experience. Then, the covid-19 pandemic put the nascent robotaxi business on its back foot. Many autonomous startups had to lay off workers, while others shut down completely. That gave Uber its own opening: pitch itself as the de facto app for all the robots. "“At least in our case, there was a different vision for how we wanted to operate and kind of bring this to the world versus how Uber wanted to.”" - Serve Robotics CEO Ali Kashani Yet Uber could never go all in on autonomy without threatening the millions of human drivers and couriers currently powering its platform. This conundrum has increasingly put Uber in the awkward position of needing to appear fully prepared for an autonomous future for investors while quietly trying to slow it down as much as possible. In Washington, D.C., for example, Uber lobbied against a bill legalizing robotaxis in the nation’s capital, arguing it would displace human drivers. The company pushed to amend the legislation to require AV networks to include a “hybrid human network” — a regulatory maneuver designed to force Waymo back into its arms. Waymo pushed back, and the bill ultimately stalled. Behind the scenes, Uber has also been hit by a wave of departures among its top AV executives, including global head of autonomous mobility and delivery Sarfraz Maredia, head of AV business partnerships Guy Peterson, VP of engineering and science Danny Guo, and head of legal for autonomous mobility and delivery Lando Juarez. Even though Uber drivers worry that self-driving cars will put them out of work, competition from robotaxis has actually forced Uber to take a smaller cut of each fare in certain cities — meaning human drivers are making a bit more per ride for now. In the long run, however, drivers face a much bigger risk of losing customers completely to Waymo’s app, which is already happening in San Francisco. “What we’re seeing right now — especially in cities like San Francisco, where you can only call Waymo directly on the Waymo app — is that it’s cannibalizing a lot of Uber and Lyft,” Campbell said. “They came in [and] took entry market share from Uber [and] some from Lyft. Anecdotally, talking to riders, they love Waymo... saying, ‘Yeah, I don’t take Uber anymore. I want to only take AVs.’” [Image: Serve is not renewing its partnership with Uber Eats in 2027. Waymo isn’t ready to completely put Uber in its rearview mirror. Even after January 2028, Uber says it hopes to keep hosting Waymo rides via non-exclusive agreements. Meanwhile, Waymo’s newer partnership with Lyft in Nashville, where Waymo runs its own app for core demand while using Lyft to soak up excess supply during off-peak hours, seems to point to a new dynamic in the industry. “Many digital ecosystems evolve through what researchers call ‘co-opetition,’ where firms cooperate and compete simultaneously,” Villanova’s Eley said. “The challenge emerges when customer data, pricing power, and user relationships become strategic assets. As markets mature, participants often seek greater control over those assets.” Still, if Uber continues to fight standalone robotaxi apps in major markets like Washington, D.C., and New York, the trench warfare could intensify. Another major test of Waymo’s independence is playing out behind the scenes: whether outside fleet operators — like Moove or Avis — are willing to step in and buy large numbers of Waymo vehicles. If third-party companies start spending hundreds of millions of dollars to own and manage these cars themselves, it will be the clearest sign yet that running a robotaxi business could become profitable. Ultimately, the question isn’t whether driverless vehicles and delivery bots will take over city streets — it’s who will own the relationship with the person tapping “request” on their phone. For years, Uber pitched itself as the indispensable bridge between robotics startups and the mass market. Now that the robots have learned how to navigate the real world, they’re deciding they don’t need a chaperone.

articles.title: California AG subpoenas Nvidia over worries about Huang's ties with China | TechCrunch
articles.summary: "The conduct of Nvidia and its former CEO raises bright red flags, including about the ways in which the company may have misled investors," California AG Rob Bonta said.
articles.body:
California’s Attorney General Rob Bonta on Thursday evening said the state has served an investigative subpoena to Nvidia following news of former CEO Jensen Huang’s affair with a woman who the U.S. government believes is a Chinese spy.

The state is investigating the company to find out if its advanced GPUs or confidential information may have been shared with China, and if the company had somehow misled its investors and the public.

“The conduct of Nvidia and its former CEO raises bright red flags, including about the ways in which the company may have misled investors,” Bonta said in a statement .

“My office is investigating whether Nvidia or Jensen Huang’s actions resulted in China obtaining advanced chips or confidential information — and if Nvidia misled investors and the public about this risk, in violation of the law,” he added.

The investigation comes in the wake of a messy couple of weeks for Nvidia, which has overnight come under intense scrutiny around the world due to the implications of Huang’s alleged relationship with the Chinese national, Alice Huang (who is not related to Jensen).

The Nvidia founder resigned last week after further revelations of extramarital affairs with the company’s employees. And while many tech voices have been petitioning Nvidia to bring back Huang as CEO, saying they see him as indispensable to the further development of the AI industry, the company’s new chair, Harvey Jones, said earlier this week that Nvidia had no intention of reinstating Huang to his position.

The company’s board has hired a law firm as well as an independent slate of directors to investigate the extent of the damage, and the U.S. government is trying to find out the extent of Alice Huang’s ties with the Chinese government.

The U.S. Congress is also gearing up to subpoena Huang, seeking questions about the affair, and the SEC is said to be launching a civil probe into the company, trying to find out if Nvidia’s public disclosures could have misled investors.

Democratic representatives have also opened an inquiry into the Trump administration’s management of Nvidia’s chip sales to China. In a scathing letter to Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, Democrats last week asked the Commerce Department to preserve records about an arrangement that they called questionable and illegal.

“Nvidia is in a messy, transnational situation but the underlying principle of our corporate securities law is clear: Companies cannot mislead their investors,” Bonta wrote.

Huang has agreed to testify before Congress after several senior lawmakers threatened to subpoena him.

articles.title: Behind Jensen Huang’s exit, questions about a management style reportedly built on fear | TechCrunch
articles.summary: Elon Musk may have been overstating it when he said Nvidia’s employees “love” the ousted Jensen Huang.
articles.body:
Earlier this week at the DealBook conference in New York, Elon Musk, beamed in from a trip to China with President Donald Trump, was asked about the ouster of his longtime friend, former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang. Musk compared it to kicking Michael Jordan off the Chicago Bulls’ roster during his historic run. Of Nvidia’s employees, he said, “They love [Huang]. They love him.”

Well, maybe not all of them. Thousands of employees have signed a letter asking for Huang’s return, but others tell The New York Times he ruled through praise and fear, as well as by humiliating people.

According to the Times, Huang told subordinates that Nvidia’s wealth meant it wasn’t possible to motivate employees with money, so humiliation was the only lever left. He reportedly told one executive his mother should have aborted him and told another employee he would rip his arms off and beat him to death with them.

Naturally, over a 33-year career, regrettable things may have been said, but the Times found a long paper trail that suggests the incidents weren’t isolated. In 2005, for example, Michael Winston, a former HR chief, threatened to sue and called Huang’s conduct the most abusive he’d seen. Nvidia paid him more than $1 million. Huang’s spokesman calls the allegations fabrications.

articles.title: Six AI-powered gadgets that could make your home office smarter | TechCrunch
articles.summary: From notetakers to webcams, here are six AI-powered gadgets to upgrade your workspace.
articles.body:
Tech companies are racing to figure out how AI can make everyday work a little easier.

From notetakers to webcams that follow your movements, here are six AI-powered gadgets worth checking out if you want to upgrade your workspace.

If you’re constantly scribbling notes during meetings, the Flowtica Scribe could save you from having to type everything up afterward.

The AI-powered pen combines traditional handwriting with audio recording. You can use its built-in gel pen to take notes, tap the side to highlight important points, and press the end of the pen to start recording audio. Once the meeting is over, its AI can transcribe the conversation, summarize key takeaways, and create a to-do list based on what was discussed.

You can even ask the AI questions about the meeting to find specific information without having to go through the entire recording.

The Scribe comes with a built-in microphone and 32GB of onboard storage. It can also identify up to 15 different speakers and supports 92 languages.

Anker’s AI-powered recording pin, Soundcore Work , is designed to capture conversations, meetings, and quick voice memos without taking up much space on your desk.

Priced at $159 (currently reduced to $99 in the Amazon Black Friday sale), the coin-sized device comes with a puck-shaped charging case and can record for up to eight hours on a single charge, extending to 32 hours when used with its case. Anker also claims a recording range of up to 5 meters, making it useful for capturing conversations around a meeting table.

The companion app handles transcription and uses AI to turn recordings into more organized notes and summaries. Users also get 300 minutes of free audio transcription each month.

If you need more recording capacity or access to additional AI features, Anker offers optional subscription plans, including Pro ($99 per year) and Unlimited ($239 per year).

The keypad can be configured to work with tools such as GitHub Copilot and Claude Code, along with a range of popular productivity and creative apps, such as OpenAI Codex, Microsoft Teams, PowerPoint, Excel, Notion, Slack, Photoshop, Final Cut Pro, Zoom, and Figma.

Amazon’s Kindle Scribe Colorsoft brings color to the company’s digital notetaking lineup and offers some neat AI features designed to clean up your messy notes.

Starting at $479 , the device is aimed at people who regularly work with digital documents, including students, researchers, and professionals who prefer annotating files rather than printing them out. It lets you highlight important passages, mark up documents, organize handwritten notes, and sketch out ideas.

Notably, the Scribe Colorsoft incorporates AI-powered tools to clean up messy handwriting, straighten highlighting and underlining, summarize notes, and help turn scattered thoughts into more organized information. Its search feature can look across your saved notes to find specific details and help identify connections between different entries.

If you’re tired of adjusting your webcam during video calls, Insta360’s Link 2 Pro aims to take care of that for you.

Priced at $249 (discounted to $199 for Black Friday ), this AI-powered webcam combines 4K video capture with intelligent tracking and automatic framing. Its smart video tracker can follow your movements and adjust the camera’s position to keep you in view, even when you move around your workspace, which is particularly useful for people who regularly give presentations, teach online, or switch between sitting at their desk and standing during video calls.

The camera also offers group tracking, which can come in handy during team meetings or presentations involving multiple people. AI-powered noise cancellation is another useful addition, helping reduce distracting background sounds during calls.

Your desk could probably use a little intelligence, too. Autonomous Desk Pro is an adjustable standing desk designed to encourage healthier habits throughout the workday.

Beyond switching between sitting and standing positions, the AI-powered desk uses built-in sensors to monitor your activity and remind you when it’s time to move, stretch, or change positions. It can track how much time you spend sitting versus standing, giving you a better idea of your daily work habits.

The AI features go a step further by allowing you to ask questions about your activity. For example, you can check how long you’ve been sitting, compare your activity with the previous day, or get information about the room’s CO2 levels to help determine whether it’s time to open a window.

articles.title: Teenage Engineering’s first CD player puts the spinning disc on display
articles.summary: Teenage Engineering has launched a new broadcast series starting with its EP/BC-1 CD player with Bluetooth and Auracast wireless streaming support.
articles.body: Teenage Engineering announced what it describes as “a modern take on a classic CD player” with its new EP/BC–1 featuring a slab-like design that leaves the spinning disc exposed instead of hiding it under a lid or inside a slide-out tray. The company says the EP/BC–1 is the first entry in its new broadcast series of products and was designed to bring “physical audio formats into a modern context, evolved from a shared obligation within the company to preserve the formats they grew up with.” The EP/BC-1 is available now through Teenage Engineering’s online store for $299. The CD player joins the company’s existing EP–series of audio devices and has the same dimensions as its KO II synthesizer that launched in 2023 so it can be paired with, and connected to, other Teenage Engineering gear including the recently-announced EP-35 battery-powered amp. [Image: Although it’s designed to play a nearly 45 year old medium, the EP/BC-1 features modern conveniences like variable speed playback, cue markers, a jog wheel for forward and reverse search, and built-in beat detection. There’s a very retro-looking series of digital displays showing track, index, time information, and audio levels, and around the edges you’ll find both digital and analog audio connections including a headphone jack and a USB 2.0 port. If you want to go completely wireless the CD player has a rechargeable battery and supports both Bluetooth connections to headphones and Auracast streaming to multiple devices that support it. The EP/BC-1 is compatible with standard CDs as well as discs full of MP3 files, and when using the former it can rip tracks to 44.1 Hz/16-bit WAV files. If you want MP3s or other formats, you’ll need to convert them yourself.

articles.title: Google says it’s going to shut off Google Assistant on smart speakers next year
articles.summary: Google is announcing some significant changes to its smart home software. Starting next year, the company will shut down the Nest app in favor of the Google Home app and retire Google Assistant on smart home devices.
articles.body: Google is announcing some significant changes to its smart home software. Starting next year, the company will shut down the Nest app in favor of the Google Home app and retire Google Assistant on its smart home devices. The Nest app shutdown takes place on January 25th, 2027, meaning you’ll have to manage your Nest products, including Nest thermostats, cameras, and Nest Protect alarms, from the Google Home app instead. If you get the Google Home app set up, Google will move over your Nest devices, including cameras and video history, to the Home app on that January 25th date. The company will also automatically transfer Nest Aware (1st Gen) subscriptions to Google Home Premium. Google says it will begin deleting Nest account data on March 25th, 2027. The changes for Google Assistant will take place later: On August 2nd, 2027, the Gemini for Home voice assistant will replace Google Assistant on smart speakers and smart displays, the company says. Google argues that Gemini for Home allows users to ask more complex questions and speak naturally instead of needing to use dedicated commands or specific language. Gemini for Home was announced last year, so it’s not exactly a shock that Google is going to move on from Google Assistant in the smart home (especially when the company also killed Google Assistant on phones earlier this year). The company says it plans to share more updates about the changes ahead of the August 2027 transition.

articles.title: Multiplying your Switch 2’s storage costs less than usual right now
articles.summary: Sandisk and Samsung’s 256GB and 512GB microSD Express cards for the Nintendo Switch 2 currently start at around $44.99 for Black Friday.
articles.body: Expanding your Nintendo Switch 2’s 256GB of built-in storage with a microSD card is pricier than it was with Nintendo’s original console. That’s because microSD Express cards, while physically identical to ones you might have lying around, have faster read and write speeds. Thankfully, Samsung’s 256GB model has dropped to $44.99 at Amazon ahead of Black Friday, which is a few bucks off its usual price but still well below its $79.99 MSRP. Sandisk’s 256GB card, meanwhile, is available for $49.99 ($10 off Amazon’s typical list price) from Amazon and Sandisk, if you prefer one brand over the other for some reason. For those who don’t want to think about upgrading their Switch 2’s storage again, both brands’ 512GB microSD Express cards are selling for a fair $99.99 on Amazon. That gives you double the storage for roughly twice the price of a 256GB card, as it should be. [Product: Samsung P9 microSD Express Card | [Product: Sandisk microSD Express card | I suspect the 256GB option will be enough for most Switch 2 players, unless you buy a lot of games. The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake is 24.9 gigabytes, for example. Other Nintendo-developed games tend to be similar in install size, though it’s all over the place for third-party game makers; Resident Evil Requiem (which also recently dropped to $39.99 on Amazon) is relatively small at 28.7 gigs, while The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt — Remastered is about 50. Some games take up even more storage.

articles.title: Eufy’s Omni C28 is 53 percent off ahead of Black Friday
articles.summary: Eufy’s Omni C28 is $379.99 ($420 off) ahead of Black Friday at multiple retailers. That’s a new low price on our top robot vacuum pick for smaller homes.
articles.body: Hosting Thanksgiving can be fun, but cleaning up afterwards? Not so much. Eufy’s Omni C28 robot vacuum / mop hybrid can help, and thanks to an early Black Friday deal, you can pick it up at a new low price of $379.99 ($420 off its original price) at Amazon, Best Buy, or directly from Eufy (with code WS24C28200NEW1). While this model has dropped to around $499.99 a few times before, it commonly sells for a lot more, making now a great time to consider buying one. [Product: Eufy Omni C28 | The Verge’s smart home reviewer Jennifer Pattison Tuohy named the Eufy Omni C28 one of her top picks after testing 16 robot vacuum mops. She thinks it’s a particularly great fit for apartments and smaller homes. It offers features typically found in pricier flagship models, including a multifunction dock that automatically washes the mop roller with hot water and dries it with hot air, yet it doesn’t take up too much space. The robot itself is also relatively narrow and maneuvers easily around furniture and into tight spaces. It boasts excellent navigation, and had no trouble climbing over the legs of Jen’s lounger, which have tripped up many of the more expensive models she’s tested. The Omni C28 also does a great job cleaning with its mops, particularly on hardwood floors. Surprisingly, it’s powerful enough to lift up dried oatmeal. Unlike most other robot vacuums Jen’s tested, this one lacks a camera, making it a good option if you’re concerned about privacy. Unfortunately, the trade-off is mediocre obstacle detection, so you’ll want to pick up socks and cables before running it.

articles.title: A UK customer ordered a £544 phone from Amazon, but the package went missing. When he requested a refund, Amazon asked him to return a phone he had never received while continuing to charge him £108 monthly instalments
articles.summary: A customer in London was left without a £544 smartphone and out of pocket after an Amazon delivery went missing, with the company's tracking system
articles.body: A customer in London was left without a £544 smartphone and out of pocket after an Amazon delivery went missing, with the company's tracking system indicating that the package might be lost. When he requested a refund, Amazon's customer service process reportedly led to his order being registered as a return, even though he maintained that the phone had never arrived. The situation became more complicated when Amazon had already collected two monthly installments of £108, amounting to £216. After encountering difficulties resolving the issue through the company's customer service channels, the customer approached The Guardian. Following the newspaper's intervention, Amazon issued a refund within four hours and offered him an additional £50 voucher.Amazon's tracking system flagged the parcel as potentially lostThe incident was reported by The Guardian on January 12, 2026, in its consumer affairs coverage. The customer, identified only as SH, had ordered a smartphone worth £544 through Amazon UK.When the delivery failed to arrive, Amazon's tracking system indicated that the package might be lost and gave him the option of requesting a refund. However, when he contacted customer service, he was reportedly told to wait another seven days before proceeding with the claim.After waiting, SH attempted to submit an incident report as instructed. Amazon asked him to use the email address associated with his account, but the report was rejected because the email allegedly did not meet the company's security requirements.Customer faced difficulties completing Amazon's verification processThe customer then tried using an alternative email address, but Amazon would not accept it because it was not linked to his account. This left him unable to complete the incident-report process through either route.The problem escalated when his Amazon order page showed that he had requested to return the phone. It stated that a refund would be issued once the product was sent back, despite his repeated assertion that the device had never been delivered.This effectively left him facing a return requirement for an item he said he did not possess.Amazon had already collected two monthly instalmentsThe financial implications added to the customer's frustration. The £544 smartphone was being paid for in monthly instalments of £108, and Amazon had already collected the first two payments, amounting to £216.The customer was therefore left paying for a product he said he had never received while trying to navigate the company's refund and verification procedures. The Guardian report did not specify whether any further instalments were collected during the dispute.It also did not identify the smartphone model or disclose the financing provider involved in the instalment arrangement.Amazon issues refund After encountering difficulties resolving the issue through Amazon's customer service channels, SH sought assistance from The Guardian.Following the newspaper's intervention, Amazon issued the refund within four hours. The company also offered him a £50 voucher as a goodwill gesture.Responding to the complaint, Amazon said: "We are sorry for the inconvenience our mistake has caused."The company did not provide a detailed public explanation of why its system had recorded a return request for a phone the customer said he had never received or why the verification process had prevented him from completing his claim.What are UK consumers' rights when an online delivery goes missing?The incident also raises questions about consumer protection when online purchases fail to arrive. Under the UK's Consumer Rights Act 2015, retailers are generally responsible for goods until they come into the physical possession of the customer or someone authorised by them to receive the delivery.Section 28 of the Act requires retailers to deliver goods without undue delay and, unless another delivery period has been agreed, within 30 days. If a retailer fails to meet the applicable delivery obligations, consumers may have the right to cancel the order and obtain a refund, depending on the circumstances.Section 29 establishes that the risk of loss or damage generally remains with the retailer until the consumer takes physical possession of the goods. An exception applies where the consumer independently commissions a carrier that was not offered as an option by the retailer.This means that when a retailer arranges delivery and a parcel goes missing before reaching the customer, responsibility generally remains with the retailer.Fearless legend or grounded realist? articles.summary: After a strong debut season, Pitch To Get Rich is back with a fashion-only edition. Season 2 of the show and will premiere on December 4, 2026.
articles.body: After a strong debut season, Pitch To Get Rich is back with a fashion-only edition. Season 2 of the show and will premiere on December 4, 2026. This season will feature 20 fashion entrepreneurs from across India.From clothing labels and accessory brands to lifestyle and design-led ventures, the founders will pitch their businesses before a panel of investors, fashion experts and public figures. Unlike a regular reality show, the format stays focused on business. Founders will have to explain their business model, defend their pricing, talk about their customer base, and lay out a clear plan for growth. The panel, in turn, will question them on everything - from margins and market fit to long-term sustainability.At the centre of the season is an investment pool of Rs 100 crore. The money will not be handed out easily. Each pitch will be judged on whether the brand has the potential to scale beyond a good idea.The season will also bring together a panel from entertainment, fashion and business, ensuring the founders get feedback that goes beyond just creativity.Speaking about the new season, actor Akshay Kumar said, “Fashion is full of people who have a great eye and a great idea. But building a business is a different game altogether. What I enjoy about ‘Pitch To Get Rich’ is watching that moment when someone must put their idea on the table and convince people to believe in it. articles.title: Whoever does television can work in any medium, says Aditi Sharma
articles.summary: Aditi Sharma believes that taking a break between projects is as important as choosing the right role, giving her the space to explore new mediums and
articles.body: Aditi Sharma believes that taking a break between projects is as important as choosing the right role, giving her the space to explore new mediums and avoid creative saturation. After nearly a decade in television, the Katha Ankahee actress says, “I’ve always taken breaks in between my shows because one can get saturated working on TV every day.”Ask her if that brings along insecurity and she replies, “Insecurity does kick in, but with time, we learn that it’s part and parcel of this career. During my breaks, I work in other mediums. I have a family, so I give a lot of time to them.”Talking about not wanting to be restricted to conventional roles, Aditi says, “Almost all my roles in TV shows have been unconventional. That’s what I look for as an actor. There’s got to be some challenge. I don’t want to do saas-bahu dramas,” she says.‘In films, you get a lot of time to prepare’Currently seen in Shayad Yahi Hai Pyaar, the actress says television has helped her develop skills which have come handy across mediums. “In films, you get a lot of time to prepare. You do two scenes in a day and you’ve rehearsed them so many times. That’s not the case in television, the pace is hectic. I have realised that whoever does television can work in any medium.”Get the latest TV News, TV Shows and more. Download the TOI app.
